lines.text: Two ancient civilizations meet on a football pitch in Houston. Egypt and Iran — two football-obsessed nations chasing the same thing: respect on the world stage.
Before the first whistle, a question drifts in on the desert wind. Long before this team, something gave this land its breath. Hold on to that sound.
Welcome back to WorldCup twenty-six Legends — episode sixty-seven. Egypt, versus Iran. Group G. The Desert Derby.
The Pharaohs against the Falcons of Persia. Two kings — Salah and Taremi — two heroes who built empires in Europe, now carrying nations that breathe football.
Egypt — the Pharaohs. Red, white and black, a hundred and ten million dreams, a nation one tournament from standing beside the pharaohs of old.

Mohamed Salah carries them all. He grew up in Nagrig, riding five hours by bus to training. Now he is Liverpool's greatest ever scorer — and at thirty-three, he knows this is his last chance at immortality.
Omar Marmoush brings the speed, Trezeguet the menace down the flank, Zizo the guile, and Elneny the calm. A team built around one king.
Iran — Team Melli. Green, white and red, the patience and pride of a nation that, four years ago, brought the mighty to their knees and refused to be overlooked.
Mehdi Taremi — the Iranian Ronaldo. His journey from a gas station to the Champions League is a story Hollywood would reject as too implausible. Azmoun hunts beside him; Jahanbakhsh brings the spark.
So here it is. The King of Nagrig against the Gas-Station Ghost. Two ancient peoples, two desert kings, chasing the same elusive dream.
And one duel defines the night — Salah's left foot, against the rise of Taremi. The cut inside the world has watched a thousand times, against a striker who refuses to be denied his moment.
And before the moment that turns a stadium silent — stay with me. Because first, Iran make Egypt suffer.
Here is how we see it. Iran press, Taremi threatens — but the King is waiting for his single, perfect chance.
Team Melli surge forward, the green-and-white end roaring, and Taremi rises to meet a cross — a header flashing just inches wide of the far post. The closest of margins.
Iran keep coming, wave after wave, and Egypt absorb it, patient and unbroken, the red shirts waiting for the storm to pass.
And then, the seventy-first minute. Salah receives on the right wing — and you already know what is coming. He cuts inside, that devastating signature move, onto his left foot.
Taremi watches, helpless. The ball bends, the keeper dives — and it kisses the inside of the post and crosses the line. Egypt one, Iran nil — and a nation weeps.
Salah sinks to his knees. Taremi stands, watching, a warrior who understands exactly what he has just seen. Two desert kings, and tonight one shadow stretches across the other.
Iran pressed and went within an inch. Egypt waited, and struck once, with the precision of a king. By a single moment of genius, the Pharaohs hold.
That is our prediction — Egypt, one to nil. The Pharaoh's shadow stretched longer. Not played yet — the real ninety minutes are yours to watch.
Because when two ancient peoples send their kings to meet, the desert asks its oldest question — is it the one who scores who is remembered, or the one who vows the sand will shift again?
Two kings, one desert, one shared dream. Tonight the post chose Egypt. The wind, as ever, makes no promises.
Do you agree? Comment MASR if the Pharaohs' king settles it. Comment IRAN if Team Melli deserved more than the width of a post.

That sound. Long before this team, this land had the ney — the reed flute whose breath has drifted over the Nile for five thousand years. That breath became a nation's song. Legend sixty-seven. The Ney Player. The breath of the Nile.
The players carry the dream. The Ney Player carries the breath beneath it. This Legend is not just to watch — it is yours to claim and collect.

Then pick three of the forty-eight nations, and every goal they score, scores for you. Free to play, just for fun. No prizes — only glory.
